title: Errors in scripts
summary: Check the steps that matter yourself; know what set -e and pipefail catch, and what they miss.

text: Every command ends with a status: 0 when it worked, another number when it didn't. A script reads it to decide what comes next.
- if ! cmd runs cmd and takes the road when it failed. cmd || die does the same on one line.
- die is the template's: the message on stderr, then exit 1.

scheme: set -e     stops at a command that fails…
if cmd; then    a failure here is an answer
text: set -e stops a script at the first command that fails. It's a safety net, with holes.
- In if, while, && and ||, a failure is an answer: set -e lets it go, even inside functions called from there.
- ((n++)) gives the old value: 0 counts as false, so the first count stops the script.
- Check what matters yourself. If you add set -e too, know where it doesn't look.
x=$(cmd) keeps cmd's status: || and if see the failure.
- ✘ local x=$(cmd): local, export and readonly are commands too, so the status you get is local's, and local always works.
- Declare first, assign on the next line: the failure comes back.

scheme: status: sort's, 0, even with no app.log
status: the last stage that failed (2)
cmd | head -n 1  may now fail with 141:
head stopped reading, cmd got SIGPIPE
text: A pipeline's status is its last command's: a failure earlier in the pipe is lost.
- set -o pipefail keeps it: the pipeline fails when any stage fails.
- It also counts a writer that head cut short (status 141). Turn it on where you check pipes, and remember that case.
